articles.summary: NEW DELHI: American brokerage JP Morgan expects the Nifty 50 to rise around 12 per cent to 29,000 points by the end of 2027, citing improving corporate
articles.body: NEW DELHI: American brokerage JP Morgan expects the Nifty 50 to rise around 12 per cent to 29,000 points by the end of 2027, citing improving corporate earnings, resilient domestic consumption, lower oil prices and a broadening private investment cycle.The brokerage has set a target of 29,000 for the benchmark index, while its bull- and bear-case targets stand at 31,000 and 22,000, respectively, according to a note by analysts led by Rajiv Batra, as quoted by Reuters."Indian equities enter 2027 with support from improving corporate profitability, easing oil prices, resilient consumer demand, strong domestic credit growth, and a broadening private capex cycle," JP Morgan said.The brokerage expects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to raise interest rates by 25 basis points each in its December, February and April monetary policy reviews, taking the cumulative increase to 75 basis points.It also expects earnings growth for companies in the MSCI India index to accelerate to 14 per cent in 2027 from 12 per cent in 2026.JP Morgan said lower crude oil prices and a firmer rupee could reduce import costs, improve corporate margins and support earnings growth. Private capital expenditure is also broadening, with listed companies increasing spending by 25 per cent in the first half of FY27, led by smaller firms and industries supported by government policies.The brokerage also pointed to the potential consumption boost from the rollout of the 8th Pay Commission. It estimates that the implementation could put Rs 7.2 lakh crore into the hands of around 1.2 crore government employees and pensioners by FY29. Premiumisation and welfare spending are expected to provide further support to consumption.India's digital economy is projected to account for 20 per cent of gross value added by 2029-30, which could support growth across agriculture and manufacturing, the brokerage said.Foreign inflows, AI diversification in focusJP Morgan sees scope for substantial foreign investment in Indian equities, estimating that the market could attract another $100 billion if foreign long-only investors restore their exposure to India to benchmark weights.The brokerage said Indian equities were emerging as a potential safe haven for investors seeking to diversify their portfolios away from AI-heavy markets."India is not competing with AI-heavy markets - it is offering diversification from them," it said, as quoted by PTI.The outlook follows a recovery in domestic equities after a 15.1 per cent decline earlier this year, with falling oil prices and renewed foreign buying supporting the rebound.Foreign investors have returned to Indian equities in November, with overseas buying exceeding $15 billion so far this month, according to the Reuters report.However, the brokerage cautioned that elevated valuations, domestic policy challenges and global uncertainties could restrict further gains."The earnings story is improving; the valuation story is less forgiving," JP Morgan said.It also flagged risks from a possible increase in US interest rates, weak monsoon rainfall, El Nino-related food inflation, rural economic stress and fiscal consolidation.Which sectors does JP Morgan favour?From a sectoral perspective, the brokerage is overweight on financials, industrials, healthcare and consumer discretionary stocks, reflecting its preference for sectors linked to domestic demand and investment.It has retained its underweight stance on information technology stocks and downgraded materials to underweight, including a two-notch downgrade for metals and mining.JP Morgan said strong macroeconomic momentum, faster credit growth and a private-sector-led investment cycle could help shift India's earnings revisions from downgrades to upgrades, with consumption also expected to remain resilient.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: European Central Bank set to appoint its first Spanish leader
articles.summary: The European Central Bank looks set to name Pablo Hernández de Cos its next president, marking the first time that Spain will helm one of the world’s most influential central banks.
articles.body: The European Central Bank is set to name Pablo Hernández de Cos as its next president, marking the first time that Spain will helm one of the world’s most influential central banks. De Cos, whose appointment must still be formally approved, will succeed Christine Lagarde when she steps down in February after euro area member states endorsed his appointment, according to President of the European Council, António Costa. His appointment and that of two new ECB board members is expected to be finalized in December, Costa said on X, at a meeting of the European Council, a body comprised of European Union leaders that sets the bloc’s political agenda. This would be the first time that someone from Spain holds the top job at the ECB, which is tasked with keeping inflation in check across the 21 countries that use the euro currency. The institution has had four presidents since it was founded in 1998. Lagarde, who was appointed in October 2019, announced last month that she would step down eight months before her term ends in order to speak more freely on issues beyond monetary policy. De Cos formerly served as governor of Spain’s central bank and is now general manager at the Bank for International Settlements, an international institution that is commonly referred to as the “central bank for central banks.” He will have to contend with inflation currently running at 4%, twice the ECB’s target. He will also take over at a time of heightened bond market turmoil, particularly in France, where high debt levels threaten a fiscal crisis in the European Union’s second-biggest economy. While the ECB has so far left it up to the French government to fix its budgetary woes, it could be forced to intervene if a sharp rise in bond yields destabilizes other European economies and financial markets. French president Emmanuel Macron said on X that “a consensus emerged” among eurozone member states on the ECB nominations. Macron added that he welcomed a “balanced trio of individuals serving the stability and prosperity of the euro area, with Pablo Hernández de Cos as President and Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier on the Executive Board.” Boone is a French economist and head of corporate and investment banking at Santander in France. Markus Brunnermeier is a German economist and a Princeton University professor. He is set to replace Philip Lane as ECB chief economist, while Boone will take over from Isabel Schnabel to oversee market operations. ‘Complex backdrop’ for new leaders Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez also welcomed the selection of De Cos in a post on X in which he acknowledged two other Spaniards in governing positions within the EU: Teresa Ribera, who is an executive vice president at the European Commission, and Nadia Calviño, who is president of the European Investment Bank. “In short, a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before,” he wrote. Spain, which has transformed from a casualty of the eurozone debt crisis to the region’s fastest-growing major economy, will hold a snap general election Sunday that could see Sánchez’s Socialist party defeated by right-leaning contenders. France, Italy and Poland will all hold elections next year, which could see right-wing political parties make significant gains. The ECB’s new leadership faces a “complex backdrop” of persistent inflation, “public indebtedness,” geopolitical and technological shifts and “consequential elections across Europe over the next year,” Deutsche Bank economists Mark Wall and Michael Kirker wrote in a note Thursday. “The renewal of ECB leadership comes at a significant time,” they said.

articles.title: EU leaders struggle to agree on long-term budget, $49bn Ukraine loan
articles.summary: The bloc is holding an extraordinary summit in Brussels to discuss its budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.
articles.body:
European Union leaders are struggling to reach a deal on the bloc’s nearly $1.76 trillion budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 and agree a new $49bn loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.

The differences were visible at an extraordinary EU summit in Brussels on Thursday, where some leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget.

Most, however, wanted extra funds for important new priorities and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.

“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time, there is a series of tasks we must fulfil reliably.”

“The priorities must be a flourishing economy, the internal market must be able to develop its full potential, and we need better defence,” he told reporters.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Hungary’s Prime Minister Peter Magyar were more forthright.

“We’re light-years away from a solution,” Meloni told reporters before the summit. “We are not willing to sign off on a budget under which we would have to give more to receive less,” she added.

“Hearing the completely opposing positions in the room, the chance of an agreement today is virtually zero, but a Christmas agreement does not seem likely either,” Magyar posted on Facebook.

The new joint spending package is small compared with national budgets and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies. But it does require unanimous approval from all member states.

While the budget only starts in 2028, leaders want to have a deal by year-end because there are elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia that could complicate negotiations.

“The budget needs to be modernised and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said as he arrived for the summit. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”

European Council President Antonio Costa, who is chairing the summit that could run into Friday, called on the leaders to approach the debate with an “open mind, a constructive approach and the sense of compromise”.

He said that an agreement is needed “by the end of this year and for this we need to reach unanimity”.

Ukraine is a big part of the EU’s budget puzzle. The spending package foresees $110bn for the government in Kyiv over seven years. The leaders must also decide on the new loan and whether the costs of servicing it should be drawn from the budget.

Earlier this month, Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if no “collective commitment” was made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception”.

Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. Merz repeated his warning on Thursday and said that “we will talk about this in depth in one-on-one talks”.

“We must ensure that Ukraine receives sufficient support in the coming years,” Merz said as he entered the summit. “I don’t think anyone in Europe can have any interest in seeing new waves of refugees from Ukraine if this war does not come to an end.”

Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of $99bn to cover most of the Ukrainian government’s needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.

articles.title: New IRS audits of top earners drop sharply: Here’s what to know
articles.summary: The IRS attributes the drop, in part, to its focus on more complex cases with potentially higher payoffs.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Top earners faced far fewer new audits over the past year, a drop the IRS partly attributes to its focus on more complex cases with potentially higher payoffs.

In fiscal 2026, the IRS started 2,153 audits of individuals with $10 million or more in positive income, down about 42% from the year before and slightly below its target, according to the agency’s annual financial report .

The latest tally is about half the 2023 total, when new audits of top earners hit 4,326, though roughly in line with the 2021 level .

In the report, the IRS said it prioritized “higher-yield, more complex examinations” that could improve tax compliance, which contributed to the decline among high earners.

The drop follows a Biden-era push to boost IRS enforcement funding, but Congress has since rescinded much of that. The IRS’ audit staff has shrunk from roughly 15,300 in fiscal 2024 to about 10,500 in January 2026, according to a Treasury watchdog .

But experts caution that the story isn’t as simple as the IRS focusing less attention on high earners. That’s because new audits of partnerships and large corporations have risen over the past year, and high earners’ income can be tied to them.

New audits of large corporations, those with at least $250 million in assets, rose 44% to 2,140 in fiscal 2026, the highest total in at least five years. New partnership audits were up nearly 13% from the year prior, though still below the recent peak in 2023.

“It is hard to disentangle enforcement directed at partnerships from enforcement directed at wealthy individuals,” Jeff Hoopes, an accounting professor at the University of North Carolina, said in an email, noting that one partnership audit can potentially affect many high-income individuals.

Max Risch, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business, said the report’s figures are consistent with a shift toward more complex audits.

“These audits are harder, they take more time, they take more resources, but the return on them could be greater,” he said.

Hoopes added that fewer audits don’t necessarily mean less effective enforcement, and said it’s not clear the IRS should be doing more high-income audits.

“I think there is an argument for the IRS to be auditing where the cost per additional dollar of tax revenue is lowest, and that may not be high-income individuals,” he wrote.

Total IRS enforcement revenue rose to $96.8 billion in fiscal 2026, up from $93.8 billion the year before, according to the report. In its discussion of the results, the IRS said it expanded its use of “advanced analytics,” which help it identify higher-risk cases and prioritize enforcement resources.

The report doesn’t say how much of the enforcement revenue came directly from audits. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration found audits brought in about 7% of enforcement revenue in fiscal 2025, while most came from collection efforts.

It’s unclear how many of this year’s new audits have closed or how much money the IRS has collected from them so far. Large corporate audits can take several years to finish, according to the agency’s budget documents .

The IRS declined to comment when NewsNation contacted it.

En el análisis de las franjas horarias de hoy, destaca una diferencia de 102,19 €/MWh entre la hora más cara y la más barata, lo que subraya la importancia de planificar el consumo eléctrico para maximizar el ahorro. Con una jornada en la que casi todo el día supera los 200 €/MWh, trasladar el uso de electrodomésticos al mediodía, y evitar la franja de las 17:00 a las 22:00, puede marcar la diferencia en la factura.

articles.title: Trump calls GDP data released before midterms ‘fake’, demands investigation
articles.summary: President says it was a deliberate decision to release ‘fake’ growth numbers before US midterm elections.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has accused his Department of Commerce of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and says he wants to launch an investigation.

Trump made his comments on Thursday when offices and stock markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.

The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday revised third-quarter annualised growth up to 4.3 percent from the advance estimate of 3.4 percent it announced on October 29. Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 elections.

“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE,” Trump said in a Truth Social post without providing evidence for the accusation.

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error,” he said.

Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fail to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. Gross domestic product (GDP) figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a prescheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.

The BEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It has previously said GDP estimates can differ from the final numbers because advance estimates for quarterly growth lack complete source data on inventories, trade and consumer spending on services.

A May article coauthored by BEA Director Vipin Arora found that for GDP, the estimates released 90 days after initial estimates typically differed by 0.52 percentage points throughout this century.

“That is, over these 25 years, more complete source data expanded or contracted BEA’s estimates of real GDP growth on average by about half a percentage point per quarter,” wrote Arora and coauthor Rebecca Pocase.

Last year, Trump fired a top Department of Labor official after a weak jobs report, accusing her without evidence of manipulating the figures, a move that added to already growing concerns about the quality of economic data published by the federal government.

articles.title: Nutrition labelling push gets thumbs-up, raises cost concerns
articles.summary: Supreme Court asks FSSAI to add pictorial front-of-pack warnings for high sugar, salt and saturated fat; brands welcome clarity as distributors flag compliance costs.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Packaged food brands welcomed Supreme Court’s push for clearer nutrition warnings, while distributors sought safeguards for small manufacturers facing compliance costs and potential losses on stocks during the switch to new labels.The court asked Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to prescribe separate pictorial warnings for excess sugar, saturated fat or salt, counting total sugars. It accepted about four months to finalise regulations and a 365-day transition for businesses.Umesh Kumar Agarwal, director of Haldiram’s, said, “The Supreme Court’s direction to strengthen nutrition labelling is a welcome step. It could help make India’s food ecosystem more transparent and better informed. People are paying closer attention to what they eat these days. That makes clear nutritional information more important than ever. Sugar, salt and saturated fat, in particular, need closer scrutiny. The WHO recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy intake, salt under 5 grams a day, and saturated fat below 10% of daily energy intake.”Agarwal said front-of-pack labels can make a real difference. “They give consumers a quick, simple way to understand what they are buying. For food companies, this is also a chance to engage more openly with regulators, improve how they disclose information, and rethink how products are developed. Done well, a consistent and evidence-based framework would help everyone. Consumers would be better informed. Companies would face clearer expectations. And trust in the food system could grow.”Vishnu Shankar, promoter of Adyar Ananda Bhavan, said, “It is a welcome move, but its effectiveness will depend on implementation.” He sought scrutiny of unbranded snacks and savouries.A senior official of an MNC FMCG company said: “Everything will be in red because 95% of foods around us are high in salt, sugar and fats. The industry will have to do a lot of educational work around this. Our job would now be to make people aware of the realities of what is good, what is bad for health. Companies like us will take as a responsibility and do it.”He also said consumers would now have to decide whether taste was more important to them or whether they were willing to compromise on taste and pay more for healthier, albeit more expensive, products. Manufacturers, in turn, would be compelled to offer healthier alternatives, even if that meant some compromise on taste.Dhairyashil H Patil, national president of the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation, warned that “small Indian manufacturers may struggle to survive, risking loss of shelf space and livelihoods.” The federation sought clear rules for existing stocks and relabelling to prevent inventory losses.Arun Gupta of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest said, “The real battle now shifts to the thresholds”, urging scientific limits.Edwina Raj, head of clinical nutrition and dietetics services at Aster CMI Hospital, Bengaluru, said, “The problem is not so much lack of nutritional information as the inability to interpret it.” She said shoppers often mistake claims such as “multigrain” and “no added sugar” for assurances that a packaged product is healthy.Nestlé global CEO Philipp Navratil backed transparency in a TOI interview in August, while arguing that labels should reflect appropriate portions.(With inputs from Swati Bharadwaj)Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child
articles.summary: US children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said.
articles.body:
Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the United States two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and artifical intelligence businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the technology sector.

The world’s richest person announced the share giveaway, which is worth a total of about $18bn, on Wednesday evening just hours after SpaceX won US approval to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space .

Musk is seeking to expand SpaceX’s role in the AI industry, even as the rapid growth of computing infrastructure raises concern about its environmental impact and the economic and political influence of technology billionaires.

Opponents of data centre development were among the biggest winners for the Democrats in this month’s US midterm elections.

“The initiative clearly helps broaden public participation in the SpaceX story,” Chez Anbu, head of wealth advisory at OCBC in Singapore, said on Thursday.

“Giving children a direct economic stake in the company creates a powerful narrative around broader participation in the benefits of the AI and space economy,” Anbu added.

The Federal Communications Commission said it approved SpaceX’s satellite constellation proposal to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

Astronomers have long been concerned about such developments in space, and the American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

It warned the proposed constellation would “significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities” and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.

Children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X.

In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX company shares would be transferred next month.

“The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk would personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a programme designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly $18bn.

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.

“What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base,” said Christopher Brankin, global markets adviser at brokerage Mitrade Group.

“It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age,” he added.

Musk, whose net worth is approximately $824bn, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk said in a post on X at the time.

“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” said Musk, most of whose philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than $14bn in assets.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in October pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative.
